summary:
SPHEREx Explorer is an interactive website built to make NASA's multi-epoch SPHEREx near-infrared sky survey easy to explore for everyone. Rather than require complex archive scripting, users can load cached or live IRSA sky regions, play aligned multi-epoch cutout sequences, detect candidate sources and click any target to inspect synchronized light curves, spectral energy distributions, sky tracks, difference previews and inverse-variance weighted stacks.
Because SPHEREx's linear-variable filters sample different wavelengths across exposures, our tool performs quantitative aperture photometry directly on native FITS frames using variance and quantity masks while linking every graph point back to its original exposure and wavelength. It supports 16 timing, kinematic, photometric and catalogue-assisted physical analyses, such as Lomb-Scargle period searches, distance and transverse speed, while enforcing strict scientific transparency by reporting uncertainties, flagging quality limits and marking unsupported metrics as unavailable rather than inventing values.
By uniting interactive visualization with verifiable CSV/JSON evidence exports, SPHEREx Explorer empowers researchers and the public to investigate brown dwarfs, variable stars and potential Planet X candidates.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?
SPHEREx Explorer is an interactive web application built to simplify time-domain discovery and multi-epoch exploration of NASA’s SPHEREx near-infrared sky survey. Users enter sky coordinates (Right Ascension, Declination, and Field of View) to query spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3 data collections—or load pre-validated local archive caches—and investigate targets through an integrated workflow:

- Aligned Time Player: Reprojects multi-epoch cutouts onto a fixed north-up, east-left sky grid using a common display stretch so users can play, pause, or scrub through observation frames with exact timestamps and estimated wavelengths.

- Interactive Source Selection & Native Photometry: Users can click detected candidate markers directly on the sky image or input custom coordinates. Rather than measuring resampled display pixels, the app performs quantitative aperture photometry directly on native FITS frames using fractional pixels, background annuli, variance arrays, and quality masks (converting MJy/sr surface brightness into microJy flux density).

- 16 Linked Analyses & Image Diagnostics: Every point on the light curve, spectrum, sky track, or wavelength–time scatter plot links back to its original FITS exposure. The platform also provides background-subtracted difference previews, inverse-variance weighted stacks, Lomb-Scargle period searches, and catalogue-assisted physical calculators (Gaia parallax distance, transverse speed, radial velocity, band luminosity, thermal estimates, and Keplerian orbit checks).

Benefits & Intended Impact

Analyzing SPHEREx data typically requires specialized astronomical scripting to handle Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) headers, World Coordinate System (WCS) reprojections, and varying spectral channels. SPHEREx Explorer lowers this barrier by providing an accessible, browser-based visual environment where citizen scientists, students, and researchers can inspect moving or variable objects without writing code. Furthermore, every measurement session can be exported as structured CSV and JSON evidence files containing observation timestamps, source URLs, and quality flags, enabling transparent verification and follow-up research on fast-moving brown dwarfs, variable stars, and potential Planet X candidates.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Programming Language & Web Framework: Python 3.13 and Streamlit.

- Astronomical & Scientific Libraries: Astropy (WCS reprojection, FITS I/O, Lomb-Scargle periodograms, unit conversions), Astroquery (IRSA archive access), NumPy, and Matplotlib / Plotly for interactive visualization.

- Data Sources & Infrastructure: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SPHEREx DR1/QR3 cutouts, Gaia astrometric reference inputs, and GitHub for version control.

How Is Our Project Creative?

- Bidirectional Visual-to-Data Linking: Selecting a point on a light curve or spectrum immediately opens its corresponding original FITS exposure, bridging the gap between summary plots and raw observations.

- Built-In Resilience to Upstream Outages: Because live IRSA archive queries experienced HTTP 502 interruptions during development, we engineered a validated local cutout caching and query-recovery system so users and judges can run full demonstrations seamlessly offline or online.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

- Linear-Variable Filter (LVF) Wavelength Shifts: Even frames from the same SPHEREx detector sample different wavelengths depending on source position. Our app displays explicit wavelength warnings, enforces approximate passband matching for light curves, and avoids falsely attributing spectral shifts to motion or variability.

- Strict Scientific Transparency: We clearly separate measured, catalogue, derived, model-estimated, and unavailable metrics. When data quality, SNR thresholds, or baseline requirements are not met, the interface reports the metric as unavailable with a clear explanation rather than fabricating numbers.

Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure & Data Acknowledgement

- SI Tool Disclosure: Super Intelligence (AI) tools were utilized during development to assist with literature research, Python/Streamlit code implementation and debugging, and documentation editing. All astronomical calculations, image reprojections, and native FITS aperture measurements are executed deterministically via Astropy and standard astrophysical equations.

- Data Acknowledgement: This project makes use of data products from the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), a joint project of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology, funded by NASA.
